blocks.text: When Zscaler ITDR engages with the attacker, it immediately triggers an alert and records the attacker's activity in the event logs. Event logs provide detailed insights into attempted attacks by malicious actors who have infiltrated the network and interacted with deployed elements. Security teams can investigate these incidents, analyze attacker behavior and intent, and use the findings to strengthen threat response and containment strategies. For deeper analysis and proactive defense planning, event logs can be downloaded in multiple formats.

blocks.item: In the left-side navigation, click Investigate.
On the Investigate page, click any icon to view the event details.
See image.
In the details pane, click View Extended Details.
See image.
Select the Event Logs tab.
See image.
For each event, you can see basic event information, such as:
Timestamp: The time and date when the attack happened.
Attack Type: The attack type (e.g., network, web, etc.).
Attacker ID: The attacker's IP address.
Decoy Name: The name of the decoy with which the attacker interacted.
Decoy Group: The category of decoy on which the attacker attacks.
Decoy Port: The port number of the decoy.
Decoy Connector: The name of the Decoy Connector.
Kill Chain Phase: The kill chain attack phase (e.g., lateral movement, exploitation, etc.).
For in-depth details of the event, click any event to open its Event Details window.
See image.

blocks.text: You can add or remove columns to show additional information about the events. You can add a maximum of 50 columns.

blocks.item: Click the Expand icon.
See image.
From the side panel, select or deselect columns that you want to appear in the table.
See image.

blocks.text: You can perform the following actions with event logs:

blocks.item: Export event logs.
You can export the attacker summary and events to analyze and orchestrate actions to contain the threat.
To export event logs:
On the Event Logs page, click the Export drop-down menu and select an option:
Attacker Summary in JSON: Export a JSON file that includes the attacker's hostname and IP address, details of the decoys the attacker interacted with, first and last seen timestamps, etc.
Attacker Summary in CSV: Export a CSV file that includes the attacker's hostname and IP address, details of the decoys the attacker interacted with, first and last seen timestamps, etc.
Events as JSON: Export a JSON file that includes all fields for event logs.
Event Fields as JSON: Export a JSON file that includes all fields for event fields.
Events as CSV: Export a CSV file that includes the event ID, timestamp, decoy details, etc. You can add additional fields, if required.
STIX v1.2: Export a file in STIX format that includes event logs (supported for STIX version 1.2).
STIX v2.1: Export a file in STIX format that includes event logs (supported for STIX version 2.1).
Snort Rules: Export a file that includes the snort rules for the event logs.
See image.
The event logs in the selected format are exported to your system.
See image.
Delete events.
You can delete events when they are no longer needed. The option to delete specific events works well when the number of events is less than 100.
To delete a specific event:
On the Event Logs page, select the checkboxes next to the event that you want to delete.
From the Actions drop-down menu, select Delete.
See image.
The selected events are deleted permanently.
To delete all events, select Delete All from the Actions drop-down menu.
See image.
All events are removed.
The Delete All option removes a maximum of 100K events at a time. If you have more than 100K events associated with an entity, repeat these steps.
Mark events as safe.
You can mark events as safe if they are legitimate events. For example, you can mark an event as safe if it was generated due to testing activity.
On the Event Logs page, select the checkboxes next to the event that you want to mark as safe.
From the Actions drop-down menu, select Mark as safe.
See image.
Test a rule with events.

You can use the listed events and test them if they match custom rules created using query language. You can combine multiple events and test custom rules on them. Typically, you can test rules on events to analyze why an existing orchestration rule did not trigger, or to create new rules that would match similar events.
To test a rule:
On the Event Logs page, select the checkboxes next to the event that you want to test. You can select a maximum of 10 events.
From the Actions drop-down menu, select Test Rule.
In the Test Rules window, enter custom rules in the Rule field. To learn more, see Understanding and Building Queries.
See image.
The test results are displayed immediately, showing the number of events that passed the rule. The list of events that failed is shown separately.
